sources.title: Canada's 'Railway City' wants passenger trains back. Like in much of the country, it's not so simple

items.title: Canada's Rail Revival Runs Into the Tracks It Already Lost
items.body:
Canada is committing billions to expand passenger rail, but communities pushing to get their trains back are working with a railway shaped by decades of freight-first decisions. Torn-up tracks and lost corridors mean the network a town wants restored is not the one that still exists.

That's the structural problem underneath the enthusiasm in communities like St. Thomas, Ontario — the self-styled "Railway City" — where the desire for service runs up against infrastructure that was dismantled or reoriented around freight. Expanding passenger rail, on this account, is less about adding trains to a line and more about rebuilding the conditions that would let a line exist at all.

sources.title: Living with chronic pain at work: Supportive managers can help, but they can’t solve everything

discussion.body: The useful distinction here is between support that changes how work feels and support that changes what work is required. A manager can improve the psychological climate without touching the underlying mismatch between a job's demands and an employee's capacity on a given day.

Which is why the disclosure dilemma is so sharp. If telling your manager risks being read as reduced capability, then the people most in need of accommodation have the strongest incentive to hide the thing that would justify it.

items.title: Why "Supportive Management" Isn't a Pain Treatment
items.body:
Chronic pain is generally defined as pain that persists or recurs for longer than three months. Many people keep working while living with it, which makes the workplace a real site of accommodation — but also a site of calculation.

Research by Duygu Biricik Gulseren and Kevin Kelloway, drawing on 2021 interviews with employees working with chronic pain, found that disclosure is complicated. Some workers feared that revealing their pain would make them look less capable or jeopardize their jobs. Others kept it hidden and then struggled to explain why tasks that used to be manageable had become hard. One interviewee put the tension plainly: "I don't want the pain to define me. I want me to define me."

Their newer work looks at what supervisors actually do to shape that experience. The finding is not that good management fixes anything — supportive leadership appears to help employees' psychological well-being, but that effect weakens as pain intensity rises. Support is real; it isn't a substitute for addressing the pain itself.

sources.title: Aaron Sorkin Says Jeremy Strong Treated ‘Social Reckoning’ Co-Stars “The Way He Imagines Mark Zuckerberg Treats People”

items.title: Sorkin on Strong: Method Acting as Method Casting
items.body:
Aaron Sorkin, promoting "The Social Reckoning," says he wasn't shocked that Jeremy Strong didn't tell him about an email Strong wrote to Mark Zuckerberg — because Strong stayed in character as the Meta founder and CEO throughout the production. Sorkin's line about it lands exactly where you'd expect from the man who wrote "The Social Network": he described Strong treating his co-stars "the way he imagines Mark Zuckerberg treats people."

Optimist: that's the whole point. If you've cast an actor to play a man whose defining trait is treating people instrumentally, having him actually behave that way on set is just... rehearsal.

Skeptic: Or it's a production where everyone else is doing a job and one person has made the job about himself. There's a version of this story where the co-stars are the ones paying for the performance.

Optimist: Sorkin says he wasn't shocked. That's not a complaint — that's a director who knew what he was buying.

Skeptic: Directors knowing what they bought is how a lot of bad set experiences get explained after the fact.

sources.title: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex with drones and snipers

items.title: Trump Says the D.C. Arch Was Upgraded at the Military's Request
items.body:
The proposed triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., has a new specification. Trump said the updated plans — rendering the structure a military complex with drones and snipers — came at the request of the US military and for national security purposes.

That reframes the project: whatever the arch was originally meant to be as a monument, the account now attached to it is operational rather than commemorative. The justification offered is the military's, not an aesthetic one.

sources.title: How to tackle persistent drought: Lessons from British Columbia

discussion.body: Eighty-five per cent of a province in severe drought is what breaks the emergency metaphor. You can't declare your way out of a condition that covers that much ground.
Framing may be the smaller half of it. A province that keeps setting records for severity, extent and duration is dealing with a trend, not just a habit in how it writes its rules.

items.title: British Columbia Is Managing a Year-Round Drought as a Seasonal Emergency
items.body: British Columbia keeps setting records for drought severity, extent and duration. In 2023, severe drought hit roughly 85 per cent of the province — and the timing has shifted, with droughts increasingly arriving in spring and persisting into winter. That is how a province ends up with continuous, multi-year droughts rather than one dry summer followed by recovery. The authors of an analysis in The Conversation Canada argue that provincial water management has not adjusted to that reality. Their case is that B.C. still treats drought as a short-term seasonal emergency rather than the year-round, persistent problem it has become. The distinction is not semantic: an emergency frame implies a condition that will end, and the record suggests this one doesn't.

sources.title: German Chancellor Merz calls state election a 'disaster' for his party but vows to stay on
Germany's Merz vows to press ahead with reforms after historic state election defeat

items.title: Merz's CDU Takes Damaging Losses in Two German State Elections
items.body: Exit polls showed damaging losses for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's centre-right CDU in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. NPR reports that Merz has faced a major electoral setback across two state elections, with his centre-right party losing ground — and that the far-right Alternative for Germany made significant gains. Two state contests are not a national vote, but a governing party shedding ground in both on the same night is a result its opponents will keep quoting.

sources.title: ‘Angh’ Review: Toronto’s Platform Award Winner Is a Lush Lament for an Indian Tribe in the 1960s

discussion.body: Restraint is the harder choice here. A story about a culture being squeezed out of existence invites a speech, and Variety suggests this one doesn't give it.
Restraint carries its own risk: a waning tribe's principled chief is a quiet protagonist, and quiet can read as distance.

items.title: 'Angh' Puts a Waning Tribe's Chief Between Indigenous Identity and Colonial Modernity
items.body: Theja Rio's debut feature Angh expands on his 2021 short film and, in Variety's account, works the hidden crevices between indigenous identity and colonial modernity. It is set in 1960s Nagaland, the eastern Indian state on the Burmese border, and follows the principled chief of a waning tribe. Variety describes that tension unfolding with riveting restraint — a premise that invites a declarative, mournful film, handled instead at a controlled pitch.

discussion.body: The $43 billion is explicitly a partial reckoning, so it reads better as a lower bound on the war's cost than as the bill.
Energy prices and depleted interceptor stockpiles sitting in the same accounting is the interesting part: the constraint isn't only money.

items.title: Brent at $103, Record Diesel, and a $43 Billion Partial War Bill
items.body: Econbrowser's military-and-economics situation report opens with a cluster of pressures rather than a single story: reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, front-month Brent futures at $103 with dated European Brent having reached a high of $130, and US diesel at a record high. The same roundup points to a threat of expanding Middle East conflict while US stockpiles of precision munitions and interceptors are depleted. It also puts a partial cost reckoning of the Iran war at $43 billion — partial being the operative word. A partial reckoning is a floor, not a final bill.

sources.title: Should municipalities ban smart glasses in pools and change rooms?

discussion.body: The device is the point. A rule against covert recording asks staff to catch something after it has already happened; a rule against the glasses lets them intervene at the door.
Ten municipalities say the conduct is already covered, and they may be right. Device bans also age badly — the rule is written around one product, and the next one doesn't announce itself.

items.title: Some Councils Want Smart Glasses Out of Change Rooms. Ten Municipalities Say Their Rules Already Cover It.
items.body: Some city councils are banning smart glasses in public change rooms to prevent covert recording. Ten Canadian municipalities contacted by CBC News take a different view: their existing rules are sufficient. That is the real question, and it isn't about the glasses. A ban on the device targets the hardware; a rule against covert recording targets the act. If the act is already covered, naming the glasses is either belt-and-braces enforcement — giving staff something to act on before footage exists — or a rule that needs rewriting every time a camera gets smaller. If the act isn't covered, those ten municipalities are wrong about their own rulebooks. A council that bans the glasses is also drawing a line in a particular place: not on what someone does with a recording, but on whether the device belongs in the room at all.

sources.title: Russia wraps up first wartime parliamentary election with Kremlin dominance all but assured

items.title: Residents of Four Annexed Ukrainian Regions Were Included in Russia's Vote
items.body: The vote included residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began but still does not fully control, as well as residents of Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula Russia illegally annexed in 2014. That is what balloting in annexed territory does: it converts a claim of sovereignty into an administrative arrangement. The front line and the franchise get drawn in different places. Residents of regions Moscow does not fully hold were included in the vote anyway, which asserts that they sit inside the political system regardless of who controls the ground beneath them.

sources.title: Ukraine fires over 1,000 drones at Russia, including hundreds launched at Moscow

items.title: Moscow's Mayor Calls a Drone Wave the 'Largest Ever' Attack on the Capital
items.body: Moscow's mayor described a wave of drones as the “largest ever” attack on the Russian capital, and said there had been damage to a Moscow oil refinery and a residential building. Two claims, two different kinds of evidence. Damage to a named refinery and a residential building is specific and checkable; “largest ever” is a comparison that depends on who is counting and what gets counted. Read together, they are an official's account of a night — one that carries both a damage report and an argument about the scale of the threat.

items.title: Ottawa Expected to Seek More Power to Intervene in Federal Strikes and Lockouts
items.body: The government is expected to propose changes to Canada's labour code that would give it more power to intervene in strikes and lockouts, according to Global News.

items.body: Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, said Washington reached out to the rebels after their rapid advance down Yemen's western coast to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait earlier this month, according to PBS NewsHour.

items.body: Linda Hepner, the MLA for Surrey-Serpentine River, resigned from the BC Conservative caucus on Sunday. She criticized the party leadership's willingness to listen.

sources.title: Ben Affleck Nearly Cast Ex Jennifer Garner As His Wife In ‘Animals’: “You Just Get Baggage”

discussion.body: A near-miss is often the better story. An actor-director almost casting his ex-wife opposite himself is the kind of detail that sells the interview, and the finished film never has to live up to it.
Or the film could have gained something: two people with a long shared history acting opposite each other is hard for an audience to look away from, whatever the movie turns out to be.

items.title: Ben Affleck's Casting Search Almost Ended in an On-Screen Reunion With Jennifer Garner
items.body: Ben Affleck is the co-writer, director and star of Animals, which premieres Oct. 9 on Netflix, and he took over the lead role himself rather than stay behind the camera. As he recounts how the casting came together, he describes a game of musical chairs that nearly ended in an on-screen reunion with his ex-wife, Jennifer Garner. The reunion didn't happen, which leaves the most talked-about version of the film permanently hypothetical.

sources.title: Duncan Jones on Why It’s ‘Harder Than Ever’ to Make His Kind of Movies (and Why He Refused to Use AI for His Newest One)

items.title: It Took Duncan Jones Nearly a Decade to Get Rogue Trooper Off the Ground
items.body: Duncan Jones, the filmmaker behind Moon and Mute, spent almost ten years getting his animated adaptation of Rogue Trooper made before it reached TIFF. His account of the delay, as he tells IndieWire, isn't a tale of one dramatic setback: sometimes, he says, that is simply what the vision entails. Ten years is a long time to hold on to a particular idea of a film, and that kind of patience rarely shows up on a release schedule.

sources.title: Zach Cregger’s ‘Resident Evil’ Grossed More in Its Opening Weekend Than the First Film Made in Its Entire Run

discussion.body: The interesting question with a number like this is casting. Cregger built his reputation on original, tightly controlled horror premises, then stepped into a legacy franchise. If the opening holds, studios will read it as proof that an auteur can be handed a known IP and deliver.

One weekend doesn't prove a pattern. Opening grosses reward marketing and built-in franchise recognition as much as they reward the director, so the same number could just as easily be credited to the brand.

items.title: Zach Cregger's 'Resident Evil' Opens to $108.3 Million
items.body:
IndieWire reports that Zach Cregger's new "Resident Evil" film opened to $108.3 million, a weekend figure the outlet says makes the director of "Weapons" and "Barbarian" one of Hollywood's biggest hitmakers.

The number is the story here. A franchise reboot landing at that scale in its first weekend puts Cregger in rare company among directors working in horror-adjacent studio filmmaking.
